The ice cracked. The crack sounded like a palm splatting against the water. An arm of black water fanned behind the crack.

"Break in the ice," Greg said. Though he knew even as he said it that it wasn't just a break. "Get up." He leaned toward Nora as she was starting to move away. "Let it go, honey," he said quietly. "Go get in the car—"

"Go, Nora," Greg shouted. "Sam—where's Sam?"

Sam was across the lake, where the ice was a little safer. Greg waved at him until Sam looked up. Greg pointed. "You too, Sammy. Come on."

The second crack came an instant later, one hole over. Greg took a step away from the splitting ice. He was looking at it, probably praying, when the ice splintered beneath his feet.

Greg Hanson had never wanted to be a solitary man twice in his life. Once back in high school, when he told Nora's mom he wanted a family, right now, as soon as possible, and once this morning, driving his children to the lake and hoping that meant, God willing, he was on his way.

The problem with wanting something so bad for so long was that when it finally started happening, he couldn't shake the suspicion that he was just dreaming it. He was thirty-six years old, and in the last six months he'd gotten his wish and his divorce.

Greg was dressed for work—dark slacks and a white button-down, this week's tie—but had taken his jacket off to walk from the bathroom to his desk. It was ten degrees teasing into the teens, but the winter's second blizzard was three days past, and the mild breeze through South Front was rocky and loyal instead of bitter.

He looked up at the people passing on the other side of the street, at a man in a long wool coat and a woman in a red scarf wrapped tight around her neck, and was convinced he'd waited a hundred years. In the red drape of the woman's hair, he heard Nora giggling again.

And he was scared. He had all the day's loose ends to tie up: a round of rewrites for the Jones Commercial, a four-hour planning session with Kessler Tom, and a quick turn-around on Kelly's copy for next week's weekly campaign. In the spring, once the lake thawed, they were likely to give up the catch and let the fish go. Some winter ice fishing was like that, where the fishing community self-policed itself on "sturgeon harvest." Not spring fishing safari. On these trips he ran a little closer to the rules than the other guys, who were his friends. He caught less fish, but he also threw more back. On a couple of trips last year, he'd talked about what would happen if a monster hooked on a tip-up, should they reel it in? The consensus had been "leave it" or, in a situation like this, "leave it for your kids."

Greg waited for an eddy, then gave the line slack and lunged forward, jamming his fishing pole between his hip and the tip-up, his left hand still tight on the line, holding the fish effortlessly. He stepped backward, trailing the fish, killing it, keeping it pointed toward the hole so they could gaff it. If it had gotten free on the other side, he would have had to ask Sam to come hold the line half out of the hole. He'd wanted to give Nora the chance to gaff her first sturgeon—if it didn't break free, or the gear. He waited. He waited for the big eddy, when the fish would tire. Julie Nelson often fielded calls from concerned family members whose uncle, brother, or husband was overdue from an afternoon or morning's fishing, especially when the particular lake in question had, recently or decades ago, given up a man.

She knew Greg Hanson was overdue the day her phone rang on Tuesday afternoon. She didn't worry right away, though, because that's what she did, listened to the concern in strangers' voices. There's always a chance they just left early, she'd remind herself, and then she'd picture Sanders, stretching on the couch and asking if she had any valerian root, or maybe just popping Caracol, the narco for Benzos, into his mouth, the thought of which itself helped her relax.

This time, though, when the father in question was listed as a school-crossing guard, she subscribed to a mother's notion that no father should disappear for days without warning. That's how Julie Nelson came to the Winnegacop station in Winslow, and encountered Rasmus Reuter early on a steaming Wednesday morning.

"Has northern Winnie seen this much precipitation before?" asked Nelson in her tight, high-pitched voice, crossing the lobby of the station. Reuter recognized the flighty tone from his years living in southern Arizona and guessed she was in her early thirties. Click-clack went her heels on the gaudy tile, click-clack went the Pomita beverage cans on the young officer's computer keyboard.

"Yitzhak, please?" asked Reuter, and the officer looked up from the screen. He was fresh faced, handsome, and red-haired, the descendant of German Jews who came to Minnesota to farm in the 1870s. "Ah, thanks."

"You want a folder?" It was Officer Yitzhak Unger.

But Nora had already disappeared into the house, in no hurry now, and Sam was looking at his phone.

Greg stood for a moment outside the door, letting the cold air raise goosebumps on his arms, warm inside in a way that felt almost new. What would happen if he didn't take sides? he wondered. What if there didn't need to be a winning side?

Inside the kitchen window, the winter light sounded like a promise.

The crack ran twenty feet from his boots to the edge of the ice and then out toward the middle of the lake. It was a seam of dark water as wide as a grocery cart, and it was moving.

Greg ran. He didn't know if he was running from the water or toward his kids. The ice cracked again, a few feet behind him this time.

"Heads up!" he shouted. "Get off the ice!"

Sam was already running. Nora looked back at Greg and followed.

They made it to land as the last of the ice caved in. Within minutes it was swirling around and sinking, like dirty dishwater being poured down the drain. The thunk of wood on water came again and again as the tip-ups floated by.

For a minute nobody talked. The family stood hugging each other. Sam was crying.

"A guy at the shop said it was safe," Nora said. Her voice shook. "He said we had at least another week."

Greg shook his head. "The temperature was wrong. The cracks . . . I saw them, I just didn't know . . . I'm sorry."

Nora shrugged out of her parka. "We're never doing this again," she said, and waded across the shallows to where her phone had washed up on a rock. She didn't look back at them.

She's leaving, Greg thought. His chest hurt. This is how it finally happens. He looked at Sam, whose face was streaked with tears and snot. He took his phone from his pocket and handed it to his son. "Here," he said. "Call your mother. Tell her we'll be home soon."

An hour later they drove out of the parking lot without speaking. They were going home, back to their new houses and new schools and new rules.

In the rearview mirror, after they'd gone a few miles, Greg saw the lake one last time. It was dark water and bare trees and a promise broken, and it was filling up with the winter he'd lost.

Greg turned and saw the man's boots breaking through. He looked down, and the water up to his shins was moving fast, brown and black and streaked with grains of ice.

One of the men waved his arms and shouted, "Back up! Now!"

Greg didn't recognize the voice. There was no grudge in the man's face, no fear. Just a kind of polite urgency. They backed up twenty feet, then thirty, beelining for the sled and the last patch of hard ice they could see leading to shore.

By the time they'd loaded the kids and the fish and Greg's tackle box and made it to solid ground at the edge of the warming shack, the three men and Greg's sled were gone. The ice was a chaos of popping circles that almost sounded like gunfire.

Twenty minutes later they were in the SUV, driving for the long causeway and the highway, the fish in a cooler between them, and Nora beside Greg in the front seat, holding his hand.

Nora squeezed his fingers and didn't let go for the rest of the ride home.

A breeze had come up, and the flags on the other tip-ups, across the ice, were snapping. Then a long, deep boom sounded under his feet, not from the deep but from the ice. The lake was a few feet deep here.

Greg peered through the hole. He had no luck seeing the bottom with the light so low, but he could see Nora's tears plinking down into it, right where her nice perch had been. He unlaced his own boots. He was supposed to take them camping in April.

He looked at the stretch of ice between them and shore. Not much more than what they had covered earlier in the day, dragging the sled and pulling along the run of the crosscut tip-up holes, but the gray patch was more than half the distance already.

Greg pulled off his boots. "We better walk back one of these holes in them, or our feet are going to freeze. We'll grab the sled." He stood up quickly and shook out his gloves. Nora followed his lead, and the water pouring from the tips of her pant legs soaked his ankles. He had forgotten his slippers.

Sam's holes were further out, probably already under water. Too bad; Sam had been doing well. Greg looked back at Nora. She had shoved her gloves into her pockets and was shaking her arms, her shoulders hunched at her ears, her face red with cold. He looked at her feet. He had never seen a girl her age cry so freely. Did she like the fishing stuff? He picked up the sled, and they began walking toward the shore.

Within seconds it took his breath. He gulped water and staggered, nearly falling deeper. Ice-cold water rushed into his shoulders. He looked around, trying to orient himself.

When he looked up, he realized he was right beneath Nora, who was holding on to the edge of the hole and gasping.

By the time he turned back to Sam and Nora, at least fifty people were swarming along the landing onto the ice. They were scattering over the wide white expanse, and the kids and Greg and the few ahead of them were out of step with them in every way, by how they moved, by the way they stopped beside their tip-ups, by the way they lifted up their kids or reached for them, by the way they held down their cap brims and their dog leashes and their poles. They were alone and out of sync. Nothing would happen to Nora and Sam, but suddenly that was all Greg could believe. They'd never know what it was like to think they were in step. In the evening, they'd make it home past the highway shore construction, past the widening traffic stream. Nora would complain about the distance and go hide in her room. Sam would grab the remote on the couch and fall asleep to the Knicks. Greg would stand in the kitchen and think how much he was going to have to pay his ex-wife to help the kids while he was out of town, buying pizza for the customers working late on his mechanic's job, and wonder if it was the right thing to do, being a father, being away from them, being close to them. And while he worried over there, over them, he'd forget that something like the snow-covered beach that spread out in front of him was waiting. And he'd forget about the cars backing in, and the people walking along the landing that narrowed, the cars pulling up along the shore, the people coming in fast behind him. If ice is going to fail, there is no advanced warning.

He had a sudden, disorienting feeling that he was floating in a dream. As the feeling peeled away, he was back on the ice, looking down and trying to focus on what, a few minutes ago, had been the bottom of Lake Winnemac.

He could see fish swimming to stay, mouths opening and closing. They were as surprised as he was, waiting at his back door.

The ice was so cracked he couldn't see a piece, but for some crazy reason it all held him up ten feet off the bottom. The ground beneath and around him was darker, more solid than the white wall between his feet and his stunned sons' faces above. He had seen the bottom of a lake only once before, on summer trips with his own father. He had thrashed desperately for ten seconds to get back to his feet, then finally stopped fighting and saw he was on an unseen chair, ten feet off the floor, in a white sock of air. The icy chill as his body melted the air around him was as cold as he had ever felt.

He waited, six or eight seconds, for the socks to open, and the only other thing that changed was: now he was two feet off the floor. The ice was starting to give way. Greg pushed, and as if he had aimed at it, one of Nora's tip-ups fell into the water. Above him, absolutely calm in shock, were his boys. He pushed again, and one of the stakes lost its grasp on the ice and fell in. Now the tip-ups were crumbling away around his legs, falling behind him into the dark. He was frozen in place, next to a half-finished meatloaf, on an island.

Then the ice around him collapsed, and for one second, a glimpse into the future, the ice split apart like it had made him its escape hatch. He felt a deep calm. He was going home now.

Back to Washington?

Did he want that?

He wasn't sure, but it felt great.

He felt the grip of winter loosen a little by his boots, and then he was falling, the water running cold fingers over his kneecaps and thighs. His feet were soaked, and he put one hand on the ice, not for leverage, just to have some part of him touching his kids, anchors.
